stories.title: Developer Duo Pursuing $600M Dallas Hotel, Residential Project
stories.excerpt: Developers Jonas Woods and 3-O Real Estate Partners have proposed a $600 million, two-tower project called Ivy Park and The English on a 2.2-acre parcel near McKinney and Webb Avenues along the Katy Trail. The Dallas Morning News reports the project could have both a 30-story hotel and residential tower and a 20-story residential tower on a 2.2-acre site along McKinney and Webb avenues, a few blocks north of Knox and near the Highland Park border. The 30-story tower, called Ivy Park, could feature a 97-room boutique hotel and 63 multimillion-dollar condos for purchase. The 20-story building, dubbed The English, would have 90 condos that could be for sale or rent, depending on market demand. Woods hopes to break ground on the project before the end of 2028. The project still requires city zoning approvals. The post Developer Duo Pursuing $600M Dallas Hotel, Residential Project appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Jonas Woods, 3-O Real Estate Partners propose $600M mixed-use project Dallas near Katy Trail
30-story Ivy Park: 97-room hotel + 63 luxury condos; 20-story English: 90 condos for-sale/rent
Groundbreaking targeted end of 2028; zoning approvals still required
stories.summary: Developers Jonas Woods and 3-O Real Estate Partners are pursuing a $600 million, two-tower mixed-use project on 2.2 acres near McKinney and Webb Avenues in Dallas along the Katy Trail. Ivy Park (30 stories) will include a 97-room boutique hotel and 63 high-end condos; The English (20 stories) will offer 90 condos for-sale or for-rent based on market demand. The project requires city zoning approval and targets groundbreaking by end of 2028.
stories.impact: Dallas downtown infill development signals sustained demand for urban luxury multifamily and mixed-use projects in the Highland Park submarket. For-rent flexibility on 90 units indicates developer hedging against for-sale absorption risk, suggesting caution on Dallas luxury condo velocity despite strong rental fundamentals. Katy Trail proximity attracts affluent demographics; supply pipeline here will pressure new rental comps and acquisition timing for other Uptown/Knox-Henderson operators.

stories.title: With Data Centers, Lenders Are Getting a Lot More Selective
stories.excerpt: The rising profile of data centers in commercial real estate investment — and in the body politic — is making lenders more guarded about where, and to whom, they loan money. The greater scrutiny could actually turn out well for some owners and operators, while others find it tougher to obtain financing or refinancing. Bank lenders committed an estimated $121.91 billion in credit for data center properties in 2025 with an average loan amount of $1.2 billion, according to data from S&P Global Ratings. Commercial mortgage-backed securities (CMBS) issuance for data centers reached $11 billion in 2025, up 266 percent from 2024, according to a January 2026 report from the CRE Finance Council. CMBS issuance for data centers reached $4.9 billion in the first half of 2026 encompassing 9 percent of the total single-asset, single-borrower market, according to an August 2026 report from CBRE Capital Markets projecting continued lending momentum as development projects reach stabilization and seek long-term financing. Despite macro volatility that has hit the CRE debt markets from rising interest rates and higher inflation from the war in Iran, data center lending continues to advance in 2026, with deals actually getting larger, according to Chris Lozinak, managing director with Newmark’s global debt and structured finance group. Lozinak noted, though, that lenders are becoming more selective with deals as groups explore exposure limits to the sector, specific sponsors or tenants. “Lenders are becoming more picky with sponsors because as much as people like to think a data center is effectively an industrial building with an abundance of power, building a data center is is not like an easy task, and it takes groups that have deep, deep expertise in the space to be able to execute on these, deliver on time and on budget,” Lozinak said. “They want to know that the group that they’re lending to has a proven track record, and that the sponsor has the right people internally, and
bullets: Banks committed $121.91B data center credit in 2025; CMBS issuance hit $11B, up 266% YoY
Lenders tightening selectivity on data center deals due to political, geopolitical scrutiny
Credit availability diverging: tier-one operators/markets access easier than secondary/speculative plays
stories.summary: Bank lenders committed an estimated $121.91 billion in data center financing in 2025 with average loan sizes of $1.2 billion. CMBS issuance for data centers surged to $11 billion in 2025 (up 266% from 2024) and reached $4.9 billion in H1 2026 (9% of single-asset CMBS). Despite the lending volume, lenders are scrutinizing data center loans more carefully due to rising political and geopolitical concerns, creating a bifurcated market favoring established operators and prime markets.
stories.impact: Multifamily operators in secondary markets competing for institutional capital will face tighter scrutiny and higher borrowing costs as lenders divert capital to data centers in Tier-1 hubs (Northern California, Texas, Virginia). Conversely, multifamily in secondary markets with strong population/job fundamentals (unlinked to data center saturation) may see improved relative capital availability and lower leverage requirements as data center debt absorbs institutional risk appetite.

stories.title: New York City’s Rent Freeze: Where It Stands
stories.excerpt: October is when the weather just starts to cool down, but Oct. 1 saw rent for about 1 million households in New York City already rendered frozen solid. Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s rent freeze, promised on the campaign trail, has only recently taken effect, but it doesn’t mean that landlords aren’t already feeling the pain. And it certainly doesn’t mean that it won’t be defeated in a pitched and ongoing court battle. Costs are increasing for property owners across the board at a time when they can’t ask more from their tenants, which begs an assortment of questions. So here’s a breakdown of what the rent freeze is, how it came about, why it’s controversial and more. What is the rent freeze? On June 26, the Rent Guidelines Board (RGB) voted 7-1 to halt increases for rent-stabilized tenants with one- to two-year leases, in favor of restricting landlords from imposing even modest rent increases. The Mamdani campaign made big promises during the last mayoral election cycle to make the city more affordable for low-income renters, and that effort would start with a pause on authorizing these rent increases, which generally come about once a year. The last increase was approved in 2025 and allowed a 3 percent increase for one-year leases and a 4.5 percent increase for two-year leases. These hikes also went into effect on Oct. 1, 2025, and if property owners were looking forward to a little relief going into 2027, they were dead wrong. Tenant rights groups celebrate at the final hearing of the New York City Rent Guidelines Board on June 25, 2026. PHOTO: Andrew Lichtenstein/Corbis via Getty Images How does this impact owners of rent-stabilized buildings? The RGB’s determination was made based on data that found overall expenses for landlords were up 5.3 percent in 2026, but it also determined that income for residential owners was up 6.2 percent over the same period. bullets: NYC rent freeze effective Oct. 1, 2026 affecting ~1M rent-stabilized households; RGB voted 7-1 June 26
Landlords cannot raise rents on 1-2 year leases despite rising operating costs citywide
Policy is subject to ongoing court battles and legal challenges
stories.summary: New York City's rent freeze, championed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani, took effect October 1, 2026, freezing rents for approximately 1 million rent-stabilized households. The Rent Guidelines Board voted 7-1 on June 26 to prohibit even modest rent increases on one- to two-year leases. Landlords now face rising operating costs—property taxes, labor, utilities, maintenance—without pricing power, creating financial stress that is subject to ongoing court challenges.
stories.impact: Rent-stabilized housing constrain landlord cash flow and reinvestment capacity, reducing maintenance standards and accelerating obsolescence in legacy stock—creating a long-term migration of demand toward newer, unregulated market-rate multifamily. Development economics for new unregulated supply improve materially, incentivizing construction of Class A product in Manhattan and outer boroughs where market rents can cover financing and return thresholds. Acquisition of aging stabilized buildings for conversion or demolition becomes less viable; focus shifts to greenfield and major redevelopment sites.

stories.title: Dallas Law Firm Leases 51K-SF in Dallas Highrise
stories.excerpt: Lynn Pinker Hurst & Schwegmann LLP (LPHS) inked a 51,800 square foot lease in The Epic in Deep Ellum for its new offices. Westdale is the building owner. LPHS will occupy the 13th and 14th floors of Epic I, located at 2550 Pacific Avenue. The firm is expected to relocate from its current downtown Dallas offices in late 2027. The new space will house the firm’s approximately 85 attorneys and staff, with room for future growth. The Epic is a landmark mixed-use development in the heart of Deep Ellum featuring two Class AA office towers designed by Perkins&Will. Epic I and Epic II combine modern, amenity-rich workplaces. Cushman & Wakefield’s Matt Schendle, Zach Bean and Carrie Halbrooks represented Westdale in the leasing transaction, while Dan Harris, John Ellerman and Will Langenbahn of Stream Realty represented LPHS. The Epic features a collection of dining destinations, including Paparazzi Chophouse and Elm & Good, a modern American tavern and social lounge inspired by Deep Ellum’s history and character. bullets: Lynn Pinker Hurst & Schwegmann LLP leases 51.8K SF in The Epic, Deep Ellum Dallas
Law firm relocating late 2027 from downtown; occupying 13th-14th floors for ~85 attorneys, staff + growth

stories.summary: Dallas-based law firm Lynn Pinker Hurst & Schwegmann inked a 51,800-square-foot lease in The Epic's Epic I tower in Deep Ellum, occupying the 13th and 14th floors. The firm is relocating from downtown Dallas in late 2027 to accommodate approximately 85 attorneys and staff, with room for future expansion. The Epic is a mixed-use development featuring two Class AA office towers with dining and amenity programming.
stories.impact: Law firm migration to Deep Ellum class-A office signals broader professional services demand for walkable, mixed-use submarkets with dining and amenity co-tenancy—shifting talent attraction away from traditional CBD. This office absorption reduces nearby multifamily targeting of young professionals in downtown Dallas proper, but increases demand in Deep Ellum residential submarket and adjacent East Dallas. Developers should assess mixed-use walkable neighborhoods (Deep Ellum, Lower Uptown, Trinity Groves) as stronger residential demand drivers relative to central CBD in Dallas for next 3–5 years.

stories.title: Transwestern, Newquest Advancing Kyle Mixed-Use Project
stories.excerpt: Transwestern and NewQuest are advancing an approximately 101-acre mixed-use development in Kyle, Texas, that will bring together retail, hotel and multifamily uses. The duo has formed a joint venture and commenced construction on the retail portion of the development, Kyle Park, marking the next phase of the broader project. Retail will serve as the central aspect of the mixed-use center, while Transwestern Development is planning a future multifamily phase that will complement the shopping, dining and services envisioned for the property. Details on the multifamily component will be announced as plans progress. NewQuest will manage development, leasing and property management of Kyle Park, while Transwestern Investments will serve as the capital partner and co-sponsor. Kyle Park is planned as a regional lifestyle center, totaling approximately 412,588 square feet of retail space with a mix of big-box, inline and pad-site tenants. Anchor and junior tenants include Dick’s Sporting Goods, Burlington, HomeGoods, ULTA Beauty, TJ Maxx, Barnes & Noble, Boot Barn, and EOS Fitness. The post Transwestern, Newquest Advancing Kyle Mixed-Use Project appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Transwestern, NewQuest JV developing 101-acre Kyle mixed-use; retail under construction, multifamily to follow
Retail component: 412.6K SF regional lifestyle center with Dick's, Burlington, HomeGoods, ULTA, TJ Maxx, Boot Barn
Kyle Park multifamily phase planned; details TBA as retail anchors lease
stories.summary: Transwestern and NewQuest have formed a joint venture to develop Kyle Park, a 101-acre mixed-use project in Kyle, Texas. The retail phase is now under construction, comprising approximately 412,588 square feet with major anchors including Dick's Sporting Goods, Burlington, HomeGoods, ULTA Beauty, TJ Maxx, Barnes & Noble, Boot Barn, and EOS Fitness. A multifamily component is planned to complement retail and will be detailed as the project progresses.
stories.impact: Kyle (20 miles south of Austin CBD) is experiencing suburban densification driven by I-35 logistics corridor demand and Austin metro population overflow. Retail-anchored mixed-use in Kyle signals strong household formation and purchasing power in this submarket; multifamily phase will serve both construction workers and permanent population influx. Developers should prioritize acquisition and entitlement in Kyle's I-35 corridor submarkets (near SH 45, SH 130) for 200–400-unit garden or mid-rise communities targeting $1,600–$1,900 rents (2–3 year lag from retail anchor stabilization).

stories.title: Gerber Life Insurance Signs 13K-SF Lease at Two Trees’ 45 Main Street
stories.excerpt: Gerber Life Insurance, the children’s life insurance provider, has signed a 12,868-square-foot office lease at Two Trees Management’s office property at 45 Main Street in Brooklyn’s Dumbo neighborhood, Commercial Observer has learned. The new space will serve as a satellite office for Gerber Life’s technology teams, according to Two Trees. Gerber is based in White Plains, N.Y. The length of the deal and the exact asking rent were not disclosed. The average asking rent for the building is $45 to $55 per square foot, according to a spokesperson for Two Trees. Alyssa Zahler, Elizabeth Bueno and Jarad Winter represented Two Trees in-house in the deal. “Dumbo has cultivated a business community defined by innovation, collaboration and creativity,” Zahler said. “Gerber Life Insurance Company’s decision to establish a satellite presence here speaks to the neighborhood’s standing as a dynamic hub for leading businesses across industries.” Michael Baraldi and Owen Koorbusch from Cushman & Wakefield represented Gerber. C&W did not immediately respond to CO’s requests for comment. Completed in 1912, 45 Main Street is a 12-story, 475,000-square-foot office property. Other tenants in the building include global architecture firm Bjarke Ingels Group and film editing services collective Church Edit. Just last week, design firm Twelve doubled its space there to 14,000 square feet, as CO previously reported. Amanda Schiavo can be reached at aschiavo@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Gerber Life Insurance signs 12.9K SF satellite tech office lease at Two Trees' 45 Main Street Dumbo
White Plains-based insurer relocating tech teams to Brooklyn innovation hub; lease terms undisclosed
Building average asking rent $45–$55 PSF; signals tech talent attraction to Dumbo neighborhood
stories.summary: Gerber Life Insurance, a White Plains-based children's life insurance provider, signed a 12,868-square-foot office lease at Two Trees Management's 45 Main Street in Brooklyn's Dumbo neighborhood to house a satellite technology team. The average asking rent for the building is $45–$55 per square foot. Lease length and exact rate were not disclosed.
stories.impact: Tech-adjacent corporate satellite offices in Dumbo signal continued appeal of Brooklyn waterfront neighborhoods for younger knowledge workers, but lease size (12.9K SF) reflects modest headcount expansion rather than major relocation. This benefits nearby multifamily demand in Williamsburg, DUMBO, and Park Slope targeting millennials and Gen Z earning $100K+. However, single small lease has limited market signal; broader office flight from Manhattan CBD to outer-borough satellites remains muted. Developers should monitor tech hiring trends by finance, insurance, and SaaS firms in Brooklyn rather than over-extrapolate from isolated lease signings.

stories.title: Brightshore Sells 484K-SF Houston Warehouse Facility
stories.excerpt: Brightshore Capital offloaded the Port 225 Commerce Center, a 484,056-square-foot Class A industrial development in the Houston metropolitan area. Cabot Properties was the buyer. Situated on 26.5 acres at 307 and 315 Beltway Green Boulevard, Port 225 comprises two buildings: a 128,992-square-foot rear-load warehouse and a 355,064-square-foot cross-dock facility. Brightshore acquired the site in 2023 and, through its in-house development team, completed construction in 2025. The sale followed an unsolicited offer from the buyer. GTIS built the development in 2024. Brightshore selected the site in Houston’s Southeast industrial submarket for its established logistics infrastructure, direct access to Beltway 8 and State Highway 225, and proximity to the Port of Houston and the Houston Ship Channel. The sale follows Brightshore’s 2025 disposition of Champions Circle Business Park in the Dallas–Fort Worth area. Brightshore’s U.S. industrial development and acquisitions platform spans approximately 12 million square feet across the Southeast and Texas. stories.summary: Brightshore Capital divested Port 225 Commerce Center, a 484,056-square-foot Class A industrial development in Houston's Southeast submarket, to Cabot Properties following an unsolicited offer. The facility comprises two buildings on 26.5 acres at 307 and 315 Beltway Green Boulevard: a 128,992-square-foot rear-load warehouse and a 355,064-square-foot cross-dock facility. Brightshore acquired the site in 2023 and completed construction in 2025, selecting it for logistics infrastructure, direct highway/port access, and proximity to the Port of Houston.
stories.impact: Brightshore's quick exit (2-year hold) after stabilization signals strong buyer demand for stabilized Southeast Houston industrial, confirming logistics/port-dependent users see sustained demand. However, disposition also reflects Brightshore's strategic rotation away from industrial asset management toward capital deployment in higher-growth markets. For multifamily: Southeast Houston's industrial-driven employment and warehouse worker household formation supports garden-community demand (250–400 units) in 77034, 77015 ZIP codes at sub-$1,400 rents. Developers should acquire land near Port-proximate corridors to capture workforce housing demand from logistics employers.

stories.title: Leon Multifamily Building 343-Unit N. Phoenix Venture
stories.excerpt: Leon Multifamily started construction on Soltra Ironwood, a 343-unit luxury multifamily community in North Phoenix, Arizona. The nearby Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Corporation has committed to a total of $265 billion in Arizona investment across up to 10 fabrication facilities, two advanced packaging plants, and a research and development center — a build-out expected to support tens of thousands of construction and permanent jobs in the surrounding area. Soltra Ironwood is designed to serve this expanding workforce and the broader population growth it is driving across North Phoenix. Soltra Ironwood will offer studio, one-, two-, and three-bedroom apartments in North Phoenix. The community is designed to include a resort-style pool, a 24-hour fitness center, co-working space, a clubhouse event space, a dog park and pet spa, pickleball and bocce ball courts, and private garages with EV charging. First units are expected in the fourth quarter of 2027. The community is being built by LMF Construction, Leon’s in-house general contractor. The post Leon Multifamily Building 343-Unit N. Phoenix Venture appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Leon Multifamily begins construction on Soltra Ironwood: 343-unit luxury community North Phoenix, Arizona
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Corporation committed $265B Arizona investment; tens of thousands permanent/construction jobs forecasted
First units Q4 2027; studio to 3-BR units, resort amenities, EV charging, pet spa
stories.summary: Leon Multifamily started construction on Soltra Ironwood, a 343-unit luxury multifamily community in North Phoenix, Arizona. The development is directly positioned to serve the workforce growth driven by Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Corporation's $265 billion commitment to Arizona investments (up to 10 fabrication plants, two advanced packaging facilities, and an R&D center) expected to support tens of thousands of construction and permanent jobs. The community will offer studio, one-, two-, and three-bedroom units with resort-style amenities, EV charging, and a pet spa, with first units expected in Q4 2027.
stories.impact: TSMC's $265B Arizona investment represents the largest single manufacturing employer commitment to the U.S. Southwest, creating a multi-decade demand tailwind for North Phoenix multifamily. Soltra Ironwood's 343 units target only a fraction of inbound workforce (5,000+ annual new jobs from TSMC ramping); additional multifamily supply will be absorbed quickly at $1,800–$2,200 rents. Competitors should accelerate land acquisition in North Phoenix (Deer Valley, South Scottsdale, North Tempe) for 2026–2027 entitlement and 2027–2029 delivery to capture peak demand before supply saturation. First-mover operational advantage favors 2027–2028 delivery windows.

stories.title: Mesa West Provides $62M Refi for Silicon Valley Office Property
stories.excerpt: LBA Realty has secured $61.5 million to refinance a 125,000-square-foot Class A office property in the Silicon Valley town of Sunnyvale, Calif., Commercial Observer can first report. Mesa West provided the debt, while the JLL Capital Markets team of Kevin MacKenzie, Peter Thompson and Spencer Bergthold arranged the transaction. Hoony Shin, vice president at Mesa West, noted that Sunnyvale has not experienced any new deliveries of Class A office space in recent years, even as the technology sector has grown exponentially due to artificial intelligence. To wit: the availability of Class A office space declined to only 11 percent in the second quarter of 2026, the third consecutive quarter of declines, according to JLL data. “Silicon Valley remains one of the nation’s leading technology and innovation markets, supported by a highly educated workforce and significant venture capital investment,” said Josh Westerberg, head of capital markets at Mesa West. Located at 285 Sobrante Way in Sunnyvale — a city of roughly 150,000 residents near Palo Alto, Cupertino and Santa Clara — the office asset opened in 2021 and features on-site solar power generation. The Real Deal reported earlier this year the building was acquired by LBA Realty for $42.3 million in June 2025, after having fallen into receivership for nearly a year after previous owners, SteelWave and Principal Real Estate Investors, defaulted on their construction debt. Brian Pascus can be reached at bpascus@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Mesa West provides $61.5M refinance for 125K SF Class A Silicon Valley office, Sunnyvale, California
Sunnyvale Class A office availability: 11% in Q2 2026, down 3 consecutive quarters; no new deliveries recent years
AI sector growth fueling tech office demand despite broader office headwinds; strong refinance appetite
stories.summary: LBA Realty secured a $61.5 million refinance from Mesa West Capital for a 125,000-square-foot Class A office property at 285 Sobrante Way in Sunnyvale, California. Sunnyvale has not experienced new Class A office deliveries in recent years, yet Class A availability has declined to 11% in Q2 2026—the third consecutive quarter of declines—driven by exponential technology sector growth fueled by artificial intelligence. Sunnyvale is home to roughly 150,000 residents and is near Palo Alto and Cupertino.
stories.impact: Silicon Valley Class A office scarcity (11% availability, zero recent deliveries) amid AI-driven tech hiring signals structural undersupply of premium space and creates financing confidence for stabilized assets—opposite of broader U.S. office distress. However, this office tightness does NOT translate to multifamily demand uplift in Sunnyvale itself; high-income tech workers historically prefer San Francisco/Oakland neighborhoods or expensive single-family housing in Palo Alto/Mountain View. Developers should avoid assuming Sunnyvale office strength auto-generates multifamily demand; instead focus on workforce-housing submarkets south of TSMC (Gilroy, Hollister) and East Bay tech corridors (San Ramon, Pleasanton) where entry-level STEM workers seek affordable rentals.

stories.title: JLL Promotes Angela Gentry to Market Lead for New York
stories.excerpt: Angela Gentry, an industry leader with two decades of real estate experience, has been promoted at JLL for the second time this year, Commercial Observer has learned. Gentry will serve as the firm’s new market lead for New York. Gentry joined JLL in 2022 in a role that was created specifically for her: executive managing director of sales and platform for the New York tri-state. In May of this year, she was promoted to vice chairman of leasing advisory for the firm’s New York tri-state region, in which she worked to advance the firm’s growth initiatives and build client relationships. In her new role as market lead in New York, Gentry will continue to lead growth strategy, financial performance, recruitment and talent development at JLL, as well as work with leaders across the firm’s business lines. Gentry will work alongside Peter Riguardi, JLL’s chairman and president for the New York tri-state region. “Angela changed how this region goes after business, and other JLL markets are now adopting what she built,” Riguardi said in a statement. “Adding her to this team is a strategic move that will make us sharper and more aggressive in the market. I’m excited to build with her.” Gentry spent about 17 years at CBRE before joining JLL in 2022. Since then, Gentry’s team has contributed to a 131 percent increase in new business opportunities at JLL, the firm said. She’s also supported over $230 million in business endeavors. “The best opportunities come when you challenge the way things have always been done,” Gentry said in a statement. “Peter’s leadership inspires us to push the limits of what we think is possible, and we’ve built something remarkable in this market. I’m energized to work alongside him in this new role. My priority is simple: win more business, grow our share and give our brokers every advantage to do it.” Amanda Schiavo can be reached at aschiavo@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Angela Gentry promoted to Market Lead for New York at JLL; second promotion this year
Gentry joined JLL 2022 as executive managing director; promoted to vice chairman May 2026, now market lead
JLL signals aggressive NY tri-state growth strategy; other markets adopting Gentry's sales/platform model
stories.summary: Angela Gentry, a 20-year real estate veteran, has been promoted to Market Lead for New York at JLL, marking her second promotion this year. She joined JLL in 2022 as executive managing director of sales and platform for the New York tri-state and was promoted in May 2026 to vice chairman of leasing advisory. In her new role, she will lead growth strategy, financial performance, recruitment, and talent development across the firm's New York business lines, working alongside JLL Chairman and President Peter Riguardi.
stories.impact: Internal personnel moves at brokerage firms have minimal direct impact on multifamily development fundamentals. However, Gentry's promotion and reputation-building signal JLL's commitment to aggressive tri-state business development and talent retention in a competitive NYC market—likely foreshadowing increased brokerage focus on ground-leases, mixed-use, and multifamily disposition strategies for developers. Developers can expect JLL to be a more assertive capital-markets and leasing partner on Manhattan, Brooklyn, and Westchester multifamily transactions.
